title: Threads - Thread class and Runnable Interface
summary: Thread vs Runnable is a separation-of-concerns decision: Thread is the execution vehicle, Runnable is the task. Why composition wins, how start() really works, and where raw threads fail.

refs.title: #88 Runnable vs Thread in Java - YouTube

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **`Thread` is a worker *plus* a task fused together. `Runnable` is just the task.** That separation is the whole design. If you extend `Thread`, you burn your one inheritance slot to hard-wire *what to do* to *how it runs*. If you implement `Runnable`, you keep the work portable — same task can run on a raw thread, a pool, or a virtual thread without rewriting it.
What Thread and Runnable actually are

`Runnable` is brutally simple: a functional interface in `java.lang` with one method, `void run()`. It knows nothing about scheduling, priorities, stacks, or operating system threads. It is a contract that says **here is a block of code that can run elsewhere**. `Thread`, by contrast, is a heavyweight concrete class that *implements* `Runnable` and adds the entire execution machinery: a native thread handle, a stack, thread-local state, priority, daemon flag, name, ID, interrupt status, and lifecycle state (`NEW`, `RUNNABLE`, `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING`, `TERMINATED`). The trade-off is explicit: `Runnable` buys you portability and composition at the cost of needing a carrier, while `Thread` buys you direct control at the cost of coupling your business logic to a concurrency primitive.

The method most candidates misunderstand is `start()` versus `run()`. Calling `run()` directly executes the method on the *current* call stack like any ordinary method — no new thread, no concurrency, no magic. Calling `start()` does something fundamentally different: it performs a one-way state transition from `NEW` to `RUNNABLE`, asks the JVM to allocate a native OS thread, and then has that new thread invoke `run()` asynchronously. That is why `start()` can only be called once per `Thread` instance — a second call throws `IllegalThreadStateException` because the native resource is gone. The design reason is safety: the JVM refuses to resurrect a dead stack rather than silently reuse corrupted state. If you remember nothing else, remember this: **`run()` is the work, `start()` is the fork**.
The mechanism: from `new Thread()` to running code

blocks.title: Runnable to OS thread handoff
blocks.caption: How a Runnable task gets bound to an OS thread via Thread.start()
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    R[Runnable task defines run] --> T[Thread object wraps target]
    T --> S[start called once]
    S --> J[JVM creates native thread]
    J --> O[OS schedules new thread]
    O --> C[New thread invokes run]

blocks.text: Construction only builds Java objects; no concurrency exists yet. When you write `new Thread(myRunnable)`, the `Thread` stores your `Runnable` as its `target`. If you extended `Thread` and overrode `run()` without passing a target, the `Thread` *is* its own target — that fusion is exactly the problem. When `start()` fires, the JVM performs security and state checks, allocates a native thread and call stack, registers the thread with the thread group, and returns immediately on the caller. Sometime later the OS schedules the new thread, which enters `Thread.run()`. The default `Thread.run()` implementation is a one-line delegation: if `target != null`, call `target.run()`. If you overrode `run()` in a subclass, your override replaces that delegation entirely. The trade-off here is visibility versus cost: this indirection is what lets executors, pools, and virtual threads substitute their own carriers without touching your task, but it means a raw `Thread` costs roughly a megabyte of stack plus kernel bookkeeping every time you create one.
Two ways to spawn, one real difference

You have two syntactic options and they compile to very different designs. Extending `Thread` looks shorter for a toy example but locks your class hierarchy forever — Java has no multiple inheritance, so a `DownloadTask extends Thread` can never also extend anything useful. Implementing `Runnable` keeps your domain hierarchy free and lets many threads share one task instance, or one executor run many task types. The cost of `Runnable` is one extra object allocation and the need to explicitly wrap it, which is trivial. There is no performance reason to prefer inheritance; there is only a flexibility reason to prefer composition, and it dominates every production decision.

blocks.text: My opinion is blunt: **never extend `Thread` in reviewed code**. The only thing inheritance gives you is saving one line of wrapping, and it charges you a permanent architectural tax. `Runnable` exists precisely because the designers of Java understood that *what to run* changes far more often than *how threads work*. When you separate them, you can unit-test the logic synchronously, reuse it across carriers, and migrate from `new Thread()` to a fixed pool without touching the task. The trade-off — writing `new Thread(runnable)` instead of `new MyThread()` — is not a trade-off at all at scale. Composition wins on every axis that survives contact with a codebase older than a week.
How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Raw threads fail in three predictable ways, and each has a signature you can spot in logs or metrics. First, developers call `run()` instead of `start()` and then report that the system is mysteriously sequential — latency adds up linearly, thread names in logs all read `main` or `http-nio-8080-exec-1`, and CPU stays single-core while work queues. Second, teams create unbounded threads per request — `new Thread(task).start()` inside a controller — and the service dies under load with `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread` or wild context-switching where p99 explodes while CPU looks idle. Each thread reserves stack memory and a kernel entry; a few thousand is enough to cripple most containers. Third, a shared `Runnable` instance mutates fields without synchronization, producing Heisenbugs: counters that lose increments, occasionally duplicated processing, or `NullPointerException` in code that looks impossible. The root cause is shared mutable state across threads with no happens-before edge, and the symptom is non-determinism that vanishes when you add logging or run with one thread.

blocks.text: Lifecycle and interruption deserve special attention because they are where interviews and on-calls converge. A `Thread` moves `NEW -> RUNNABLE -> BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING -> TERMINATED`, and there is no path back. `sleep()`, `join()`, and `Object.wait()` all relinquish the CPU but differ critically: `sleep()` holds any monitors it owns while `wait()` releases them — mixing these up is a classic deadlock factory. Interruption is cooperative, not preemptive: `thread.interrupt()` merely sets a flag and wakes sleepers with `InterruptedException`; if your `run()` swallows that exception or never checks `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()`, the thread becomes unkillable by policy. The trade-off of cooperative cancellation is responsiveness versus safety — the platform refuses to kill a thread mid-monitor because that would corrupt shared state, so you pay by writing loops that poll the flag and clean up properly.

blocks.title: The start() vs run() trap
blocks.text: If an interviewer asks you to debug sequential behavior, check the call site first. `task.run()` is a plain synchronous call — it proves your logic works but proves nothing about concurrency. `thread.start()` is the only path that forks. In code review, flag any direct `run()` invocation on a `Thread` instance as a defect unless it is an explicit synchronous unit test.

items.title: Write both forms from memory
items.text: Expect: extend Thread with overridden run() versus implement Runnable plus new Thread(r).start(). They grade whether you call start() not run(), handle the one-shot start rule, and name the thread. Finish this in under five minutes.

items.title: Explain why Runnable is preferred
items.text: Say: single inheritance, task reuse across threads and pools, clean unit testing by invoking run() directly. Name the trade-off: one extra wrapper object in exchange for decoupling work from carrier.

items.title: Predict output of shared Runnable
items.text: Two threads sharing one Runnable with an int counter. Correct answer: race, lost updates, fix with synchronized block, AtomicInteger, or local variables. Mention visibility — without volatile or locking, writes may never be seen.

items.title: Design the follow-up: 10k tasks
items.text: Pivot from new Thread() to ExecutorService with a bounded pool, a work queue, and shutdown(). Explain why: bounded memory, amortised thread creation, backpressure. Mention Callable and Future if a result is needed, since Runnable cannot return or throw checked exceptions.

items.title: Handle interruption and join
items.text: Show a loop that checks isInterrupted(), restores the flag after catching InterruptedException, and a main thread that calls join() or awaitTermination(). This separates candidates who memorised syntax from those who can shut a system down cleanly.

items: `Runnable` creates a thread — it does not. It is inert task code until a `Thread`, pool, or virtual thread executes it.
Calling `run()` achieves concurrency — it runs synchronously on the caller; only `start()` forks a new call stack.
Extending `Thread` is faster — identical execution cost, worse design; the extra Runnable allocation is negligible.
`Runnable` can return a value or throw a checked exception — it cannot; that is what `Callable<T>` plus `Future` is for.
Threads share nothing by default — they share the entire heap; only local variables and stack state are private.
Stopping a thread with `stop()` or a boolean flag is equivalent to interruption — `stop()` is deprecated and unsafe, a plain flag lacks wake-up semantics; use `interrupt()` and handle it.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Choosing raw Thread and Runnable versus higher abstractions.
rows: One-off background worker, learning exercise
Runnable + new Thread()
Simplest correct fork; no pool config needed
Task reused across carriers or tested alone
Runnable as separate class or lambda
Decouples logic from threading; directly unit-testable
Many short-lived tasks, request handling
Runnable + ExecutorService
Bounds threads, reuses stacks, adds queue and rejection policy
Need result or checked exception
Callable + Executor, not Runnable
Runnable.run() returns void and swallows checked throws
10k+ concurrent blocking tasks
Runnable on virtual threads
Cheap stacks change the cost model; raw platform threads collapse
Chained async stages, timeouts, composition
CompletableFuture or structured concurrency
Raw threads give you no composition, cancellation propagation, or pipelines

blocks.text: For modern Java, add one sentence that signals seniority: raw `Thread` is now a low-level carrier, not a scaling strategy. Since virtual threads, the idiom `Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or an `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` lets the same unchanged `Runnable` scale to hundreds of thousands of blocking tasks because the stack is heap-allocated and mountable. The trade-off flips — platform threads are precious kernel resources to be pooled, virtual threads are cheap enough to create per task — but the `Runnable` abstraction survives both worlds untouched. That durability is the strongest argument for writing tasks as `Runnable` from day one: carriers come and go, the work endures.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Use a `Runnable` to define the work and hand it to a `Thread` or pool to run it — never fuse them by extending `Thread` — because composition keeps the task reusable, testable, and pool-compatible while `start()`, not `run()`, is what actually forks a new thread.
